passage:
"Papa, can I ask something?"
Hemant looked up from the dishes. "Of course, Thomas."
"When you and Mummy shouted last night... was it because of my report card?"
Hemant turned off the tap. "Why do you think that?"
"Because you said 'his marks' and then it got louder."
Hemant dried his hands and sat down next to him. "Listen carefully. Mummy and I were arguing about grown-up things. Money, work, how tired we are. Your marks came up for one second. But our fights are not because of you. Not your marks, not your room, nothing you did."
Thomas's shoulders dropped. "Promise?"
"Promise. It's our job to sort it out, not yours."

qa.q: What did Thomas hear Papa say that made him worried?
qa.a: He heard Papa say "his marks" before it got louder.

qa.q: What was Thomas afraid of?
qa.a: He was afraid and guilty, thinking the fight was his fault because of his report card.

qa.q: What did Hemant do that helped Thomas?
qa.a: He stopped what he was doing, sat down, and told Thomas clearly that the fights were not his fault and that it was the parents' job to sort it out.

qa.q: How might Hemant have felt when Thomas asked his question?
qa.a: Hemant may have felt sad and a bit guilty that Thomas had been carrying that worry.

grounding: A boy wonders if his parents' fighting is because of his marks; when he asks, his father tells him clearly that it is not his fault.

passage:
My name is Ramesh, and when I was nine, my parents argued almost every night. I was sure it was because of me. Maybe because I left my toys all over the floor, or because I forgot my homework so often.
So I became perfect. I made my bed without being asked. I kept my room spotless. My younger brother Omkar thought I'd gone strange.
But they still argued.
One night, Omkar asked Ma straight out: "Are you fighting because of us?" She knelt down and said, "No. Never. You two have nothing to do with it. These are grown-up problems."
I felt something heavy slip off my back. I let myself leave one sock on the floor.

qa.q: What did Omkar ask Ma?
qa.a: "Are you fighting because of us?"

qa.q: Why did Ramesh try to be perfect?
qa.a: Ramesh felt guilty and anxious, believing the arguments were caused by the mess and forgotten homework.

qa.q: What made the biggest difference to Ramesh?
qa.a: Ma saying clearly that the children had nothing to do with it and that these were grown-up problems.

qa.q: How might Omkar have seen his sibling's sudden perfect behaviour?
qa.a: Omkar thought Ramesh had gone strange, not understanding the worry behind it.

grounding: A child blames themselves for the parents' fighting and tries to be perfect, until a parent says clearly it is not the children's fault.

passage:
"Aadhya, your Francis Uncle was once the angriest boy in Bandra. When my parents split up, I was eleven. I was furious with both of them for wrecking our home.
I slammed doors so hard the pictures shook. One day I shouted at my mother, 'It's all your fault!' It wasn't true. I saw her face crumple, and I felt worse than before.
My grandfather took me out running along the sea wall every morning after that. 'Run it off,' he said. 'Then tell me in words.' Slowly I learned to say, 'I'm angry because I'm sad.' That was the truth underneath."

qa.q: Where did young Francis run with his grandfather?
qa.a: Along the sea wall.

qa.q: What was young Francis feeling underneath his anger?
qa.a: He was sad about his family breaking up, and the fury was covering that sadness.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Francis handle his anger?
qa.a: Running with his grandfather every morning and learning to say in words that he was angry because he was sad.

qa.q: How did Francis's mother react when he blamed her?
qa.a: Her face crumpled, showing she was deeply hurt by his unfair words.

grounding: An uncle recalls being angry at both parents after their split, slamming doors and unfairly blaming one, then learning to run and say the sadness in words.

passage:
Moving day was chaos. It was pouring, the van was late, and half the boxes were still open. Akash's mother, Rekha, was on the phone with the landlord.
Akash kicked a box of books. It split and the books slid out. "This is all your fault!" he shouted, then stopped. It wasn't only hers.
Rekha put the phone down. "Say it, Akash. Say what you really feel."
His throat hurt. "I'm angry at both of you. You broke our home. And I'm sad."
She hugged him. "That's allowed."
Then she gave him a notebook and a pen. "Draw it while I finish the call." He drew a house with a crack down the middle.

qa.q: What did Akash kick?
qa.a: A box of books.

qa.q: What was Akash really feeling on moving day?
qa.a: He was angry at both parents, and underneath that anger he was sad about losing their home.

qa.q: What helped Akash express his anger safely?
qa.a: Rekha asked him to say what he felt in words and gave him a notebook to draw it.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Akash blamed her?
qa.a: Rekha may have felt hurt and stressed, but she stayed calm and helped him say the truth.

grounding: On a chaotic moving day a boy lashes out and unfairly blames his mother, then puts his anger and sadness into words and a drawing.

passage:
In their flat in Malmö, Noa's mum said, "Your father never cared about anything but work. Tell him I need the money for your shoes."
At her dad's place on the weekend, he said, "Your mum is so controlling. Ask her why she won't let me come to your concert."
Noa felt stretched like an elastic band. She loved them both.
On Sunday, when Dad asked again, she put down her fork. "Keep me out of the middle. I'm not carrying messages."
Dad was quiet for a moment. "You're right. That's not fair on you."
Monday, she said the same to her mum, Ulla. Ulla nodded slowly.

qa.q: Where did Noa's mum live?
qa.a: In their flat in Malmö.

qa.q: How did Noa feel when both parents asked her to carry messages?
qa.a: She felt torn and stretched like an elastic band, because she loved them both.

qa.q: What wise thing did Noa say?
qa.a: She asked to be kept out of the middle and said she would not carry messages.

qa.q: How might Noa's dad see what he'd been doing?
qa.a: After Noa spoke, her dad seemed to realise it wasn't fair to put her in the middle.

grounding: Each parent badmouths the other and asks a girl to pass messages; she feels torn and says she does not want to be in the middle.

passage:
In the school counsellor's room, Santosh stared at the carpet. "Papa says Mummy lies about everything. Mummy says Papa doesn't care. And they both ask me what the other one said."
Rajni Ma'am listened. "How does that feel?"
"Like I'm a spy. I hate it. I love them both."
"You're allowed to ask them to keep you out of the middle," she said. "Want to practise?"
Santosh tried. "Please keep me out of the middle." His voice was small. He tried again, louder.
Rajni Ma'am said she'd also call both parents that week. That evening Santosh told Papa. Papa looked surprised, then nodded.

qa.q: Where did Santosh talk to Rajni Ma'am?
qa.a: In the school counsellor's room.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel about being asked what each parent said?
qa.a: He felt like a spy and hated it, torn because he loved them both.

qa.q: How did Rajni Ma'am help Santosh?
qa.a: She listened, told him he could ask to be kept out of the middle, helped him practise, and planned to call both parents.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Santosh spoke up?
qa.a: Papa seemed surprised at first, then accepted what Santosh said.

grounding: A boy whose parents each badmouth the other feels like a spy; with a counsellor's help he practises saying he does not want to be in the middle.

passage:
Tuesday. Two weeks after Papa moved out, Chaitanya opened the bathroom cabinet and smelled Papa's hair oil. Suddenly he was crying, sitting on the cold floor.
Saturday. He went to Papa's new flat. They still did their Saturday crossword, the way they always had. It felt strange in a new room. Hemant, his father, squeezed his hand.
The next Wednesday. In class, Mrs Menon asked everyone to draw their family. Chaitanya's eyes filled. At break, he told Mrs Menon about the separation. Mrs Menon said, "Feeling sad about it is normal. Nobody has to be okay quickly." Chaitanya didn't feel fine. But he felt allowed to not be fine.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya smell in the bathroom cabinet?
qa.a: Papa's hair oil.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel when she smelled Papa's hair oil?
qa.a: He felt a sudden wave of grief and missed her old family, crying on the cold floor.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya with her grief?
qa.a: Keeping the Saturday crossword routine with Hemant and talking to Mrs Menon, who said feeling sad was normal.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel doing the crossword in his new flat?
qa.a: Hemant may feel sad about the change but glad to keep something familiar with Chaitanya.

grounding: After his parents separate, a boy cries at odd moments, keeps routines with his father and talks about it, and is allowed to be sad without hurrying.

passage:
"Lalremsiami, sit here. Your Nirmala Aunty knows a bit about this. When I was nine, my parents separated. Nobody had died, but it felt like it.
I'd be fine, then I'd hear a song my father used to whistle on the radio, and I'd start crying right there in the kitchen. I thought something was wrong with me.
My aunt said, 'It's grief. It comes and goes.' She kept our evening walks the same, every day at six. She let me cry without telling me to cheer up.
It took a long time. But I never had to pretend."

qa.q: What made young Nirmala cry in the kitchen?
qa.a: A song her father used to whistle, playing on the radio.

qa.q: How did young Nirmala feel about crying at odd times?
qa.a: She felt confused and worried, thinking something was wrong with her.

qa.q: What choice by the aunt in the story helped young Nirmala most?
qa.a: Naming it as grief, keeping the evening walks at six, and letting her cry without telling her to cheer up.

qa.q: How might the aunt in the story have seen young Nirmala's tears?
qa.a: The aunt saw them as normal grief that comes and goes, not something to fix quickly.

grounding: An aunt recalls grieving her parents' separation, crying at odd times, and being helped by routines and permission to be sad.

passage:
"Aparna, your Joseph Uncle had a plan once. My parents had separated when I was ten, and I was sure I could fix it. I decided on a family photo day. I rang the studio and booked it myself, told each of them the other had agreed.
They both came. They were polite. They stood stiffly for the photo. Then they went home to separate houses.
I cried that night. But later I saw something. My father taught me chess on Saturdays. My mother and I baked on Sundays. Each day was good, just different.
Once I stopped trying to fix them, I could enjoy each of them."

qa.q: What did young Joseph book at the studio?
qa.a: A family photo day.

qa.q: How did young Joseph feel after the photo day?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and sad, crying that night because his plan didn't bring his parents back together.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Joseph?
qa.a: Seeing that he couldn't fix his parents' marriage and starting to enjoy chess with his father and baking with his mother.

qa.q: How might Joseph's parents have felt standing for the photo?
qa.a: They likely felt awkward and stiff, trying to be polite for their son's sake.

grounding: An uncle recalls hoping to reunite his separated parents with a plan, being disappointed, and slowly accepting so he could enjoy time with each.

passage:
Parul had planned everything for her birthday: both parents at the same table, a cake with both their names on the card. Maybe, if they sat together, they'd remember.
But it rained, the roads flooded, and Papa was an hour late. By the time he arrived, Charu, her mother, had already cut the cake with the cousins.
Papa sat at the far end. They were polite, but didn't talk.
Parul went to the balcony. Her throat ached.
Papa came out. "Birthday walk tomorrow? Just us?" Then Charu came out with a plate. "Your favourite piece, with the rose."
Parul realised: two separate, happy moments. Not the one she'd planned. But still happy.

qa.q: Why was Papa an hour late?
qa.a: It rained and the roads flooded.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling on the balcony?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and sad, with an aching throat, because her plan to bring her parents together hadn't worked.

qa.q: What did Parul start to accept?
qa.a: That she couldn't fix her parents' marriage, but she could enjoy separate happy moments with each of them.

qa.q: How might Charu feel bringing Parul the rose piece of cake?
qa.a: Charu probably wants Parul to feel loved on her birthday, even if things can't be the way Parul hoped.

grounding: A girl hopes her separated parents will reunite at her birthday; when her plan fails, she begins to accept it and enjoy time with each.

passage:
Friday
Mum sat on the edge of my bed tonight. She said she and Papa won't live together any more. I held my pillow so tight.
Then she said the most important thing, twice: "This is not because of you, Yusuf. We both love you. That will never change."
I asked if I'd still go to football on Saturdays. She said yes, and Papa will take me like always. I asked if I should tell Papa anything from her. She said, "No. You don't carry messages. We'll talk to each other."
She didn't say one bad thing about Papa. Not even when I asked why.
I cried, but I'm not scared the way I was.

qa.q: Where did Mum sit when she told Yusuf?
qa.a: On the edge of the bed.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel after Mum's talk?
qa.a: Yusuf still cried, but felt less scared because Mum said it wasn't Yusuf's fault and both parents still loved Yusuf.

qa.q: What did Mum do that a wise parent would do?
qa.a: She said clearly it wasn't Yusuf's fault, kept football routines, refused to use Yusuf as a messenger and never badmouthed Papa.

qa.q: How might Mum have felt during this talk?
qa.a: Mum was probably sad and careful, choosing her words so Yusuf would feel safe.

grounding: A mother tells her child calmly that the split is not the child's fault, that both parents love them, keeps routines and avoids badmouthing or using the child as a messenger.

passage:
On the morning milk round in their village, Ramesh stopped the cycle by the canal and turned to his son. "Vaibhav, your Aai and I have decided to live in different houses."
Vaibhav stared at the milk cans.
"It's not because of anything you did. Not your marks, not the broken lantern. We both love you, and that won't change."
"Will we still do the milk round?"
"Every morning, same as now."
"Should I tell Aai anything?"
"No. I'll talk to her myself. That's not your job."
Vaibhav didn't say much more. But he held the handlebar and helped push the cycle on.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt telling his son?
qa.a: Ramesh was likely nervous and sad, choosing a familiar routine and calm words to make it gentler.

grounding: A father tells his son calmly that the split is not his fault, that both parents love him, keeps their routine and refuses to use him as a messenger.

passage:
During the monsoon, Elizabeth was sent to stay with Ammachi in the village while her parents sorted out "grown-up things". She knew what that meant.
The first night she couldn't sleep. The rain drummed on the tiled roof. She crept to Ammachi's room.
Ammachi opened her arms without a word. Elizabeth climbed in.
"Ammachi, is our family finished?"
Ammachi stroked her hair. "Your home may look different, molé. But my love for you won't change. Nor your Amma Jaya's."
Elizabeth let herself cry then. She told Ammachi she was scared and angry.
Ammachi held her until the rain softened, and Elizabeth slept.

qa.q: What was drumming on the tiled roof?
qa.a: The rain.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she crept to Ammachi's room?
qa.a: She felt scared and unsettled, unable to sleep, worried her family was finished.

qa.q: What helped Elizabeth feel calmer?
qa.a: Being held by Ammachi, hearing that her love wouldn't change, and being able to say honestly that she was scared and angry.

qa.q: How might Ammachi see Elizabeth's worries?
qa.a: Ammachi sees them as natural and meets them with steady warmth rather than explanations.

grounding: A grandmother holds her granddaughter during her parents' separation and says her love will not change; the girl calms and speaks honestly.

passage:
I'm Nilesh, and when my parents separated in Class 6, I told no one. When friends asked why my dad didn't come to sports day, I said he was busy.
Every lie made my stomach tight. I was sure everyone would think our family was broken.
Then one day Leela, who sat next to me, said her parents had separated two years earlier. She said it so simply.
After school I walked with her and told her everything. She just nodded. "It gets less weird."
I didn't tell the whole class. Just Leela. But for the first time in months, I didn't feel like I was hiding.

qa.q: What did Nilesh say when friends asked why Dad didn't come to sports day?
qa.a: That he was busy.

qa.q: What was Nilesh afraid of?
qa.a: Nilesh felt ashamed and afraid that everyone would think the family was broken.

qa.q: Why was telling Leela a good choice?
qa.a: Leela had been through the same thing and was kind, so sharing with one trusted friend ended the lonely feeling of hiding.

qa.q: How might Leela feel when Nilesh tells her?
qa.a: Leela may feel understanding and glad to help, since she had been through it herself.

grounding: Nilesh hides a parents' separation out of shame, then chooses one trusted friend to tell and feels less alone.

Vaibhav has been quiet and edgy since the start of term. When the class made Father's Day cards, he said he'd "lost his pencil" and sat looking out of the window. I later learned from his mother that his parents have separated.
Today I noticed him talking quietly with Joseph at the back of the class during break. Joseph just nodded and listened. Vaibhav looked lighter afterwards and joined in the cricket match.
I spoke to Vaibhav briefly after school and told him he could always talk to me as well. He didn't say much, but he smiled.

qa.a: Father's Day cards.

qa.q: How had Vaibhav seemed since the start of term?
qa.a: He seemed quiet, edgy and embarrassed, avoiding anything that might reveal his parents' separation.

qa.q: What helped Vaibhav start to feel lighter?
qa.a: Telling one trusted friend, Joseph, who listened, and knowing the teacher was also there to talk to.

qa.q: How might Joseph see his role in helping Vaibhav?

grounding: A boy hides his parents' separation out of embarrassment, then tells one trusted friend and feels lighter.

I'm Tenzin, and last winter my father started buying me things every visit. A video game. A new jacket. Then a phone.
Each time he'd say, "Your mother could never afford this. Maybe you'd be happier living with me?"
It felt nice, holding the new phone. But also wrong, like a trade.
Francis, my friend, asked why I wasn't happy about the phone. I shrugged.
Finally I told my father: "I love you both. I don't want to choose. Please stop asking."
He looked surprised. Then embarrassed. The gifts slowed after that, and he stopped asking me to choose.

qa.q: What was the last gift Tenzin mentioned?
qa.a: A phone.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about the gifts?
qa.a: Tenzin felt uneasy and conflicted, because the gifts felt nice but also wrong, like a trade.

qa.q: What did Tenzin say that helped?
qa.a: Tenzin told the father, "I love you both. I don't want to choose. Please stop asking."

qa.q: How did Tenzin's father react?
qa.a: He looked surprised, then embarrassed, and stopped asking Tenzin to choose.

grounding: A father bribes Tenzin with gifts and hints Tenzin should choose him; Tenzin says they love both parents and do not want to choose.

Lakshmi has been arriving with expensive new things: a watch, fancy pencils, a new school bag. Today she stayed back and told me her mother keeps buying them. "Amma says Papa never buys me anything, so I should stay with her."

"Papa, can I tell you something weird?"
Pradeep put down his tea. "Always."
"Since you moved out, the house is so quiet. No shouting. I sleep better." Nikita paused. "And then I feel horrible for being happy about it."
"You're not horrible, Nikita."
"But isn't it like I'm glad you left?"

"I know. Both feelings can be true at the same time."

qa.q: What did Pradeep help Nikita understand?

qa.q: How does Pradeep feel about the quiet?
qa.a: Pradeep admits he is relieved too, because the quiet is better for everyone.

grounding: A girl feels relieved that the house is quiet after her parents separate, then guilty; her father helps her see both feelings are true.

I'm Neelam. After my parents separated, our flat went quiet. No doors slamming. No sharp voices through the walls at night.
The first week, I noticed I was humming while doing homework. My younger brother Vijay and I played carrom without flinching at every sound.

I told Ma one evening. She said, "You can miss Papa and still be glad the fighting stopped. Both are true."
I still miss him on Sundays. But now I let myself enjoy the quiet too.

qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: What did Neelam feel after noticing the humming?

qa.q: What helped Neelam accept both feelings?
qa.a: Ma explaining that missing Papa and being glad the fighting stopped can both be true.

qa.q: How might Vijay have experienced the quieter flat?
qa.a: Vijay seemed calmer too, playing carrom without flinching at every sound.
